extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics graduate students, and educated general readers interested in the practice and philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter describing how mathematics is practiced, evaluated, and sustained (tools, community, publication, pedagogy, and epistemology). Written for readers seeking a synthetic picture of the mathematical profession and its standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruments for recording and duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: To do mathematics one must have, at the very least, instruments of writing or recording and of duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before printing there were 'scribe factories' for replication; adequate means to record and duplicate work are a baseline requirement for doing and transmitting mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler-and-compass foundation for Euclidean geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: The ruler and compass are built into the axioms at the foundation of Euclidean geometry; Euclidean geometry can be defined as the science of ruler-and-compass constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable constructions and results in Euclidean geometry are judged relative to these classical tools and axioms; the choice of primitive instruments can define the content of a subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic aided by instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic has been aided by many instruments and devices: three of the most successful have been the abacus, the slide rule, and the modern electronic computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different computational instruments change practice and perception of arithmetic (e.g., electronic computers have relegated manual arithmetic to secondary importance); choice of instrument affects pedagogy and technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer capabilities for symbolic manipulation and graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: When programmed appropriately, the computer has the ability to perform many symbolic mathematical operations (formal algebra, formal calculus, formal power series, differential equations) and to produce powerful geometric graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite potential (FORMAC/MACSYMA cited), such programs have not universally transformed practice; computer graphics can depict objects with no real-world existence; in some cases physical models remain more efficient than graphical displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for constructive and algorithmic results
rubrics_metrics.description: There is greater interest in constructive and algorithmic results, and decreasing interest in purely existential or dialectical results that have little or no computational meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of computers and a generation trained in programming lure mathematicians toward algorithmic/constructive directions; the computational meaning of results becomes a criterion of interest and perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of physical models when efficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally it is still more efficient to use a physical model rather than attempting a computer graphics display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical engineering practice (e.g., scaled, color-coded models) may outperform or complement computational displays; choose modeling medium by effectiveness for the problem at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and meeting forums as venues for vetting work
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous regional, national, and international meetings are held periodically, and there is lively activity in the writing and publishing of books at all levels, with more than 1600 individual technical journals appropriate for mathematical material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities form the international forum in which mathematics is perpetuated and innovated and in which discrepancies in practice and meaning are thrashed out; appropriate venue selection matters for dissemination and debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community consensus as the practical criterion of importance (Ulam's dilemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: With perhaps 100,000–200,000 theorems published yearly, it is impossible for a single person to survey all work; judgment of what is 'important' thus relies on interactions and the synthesis of many people's judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no one can command recent work in more than a few areas, evaluations of importance are practical compromises requiring committees or community attention rather than universal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single global evaluative criteria across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no stated criteria that would permit us to evaluate work in widely separated fields of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fields like nonlinear wave propagation and category-theoretic logic are incommensurable by a single standard; cross-field evaluation requires panels, multiple perspectives, or acceptance of plural values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding allocation follows market-like metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: If more research proposals are made in area x and are favorably refereed, then more will be funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal agencies explicitly deny attempts to pick 'important' areas; in practice funding distribution is driven by the number and favorability of proposals (a market/public-opinion mechanism), rather than a centralized value judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and advisory decisions made by multi-specialty committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming committees of exceptional mathematicians whose ranges include several specialties is the practical way to constitute editorial boards or advisory panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such committees reach decisions not by global debate on fundamental choices but by aggregating specialist judgments, often allocating quotas among fields (political principle of nonaggression/mutual indifference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ph.D. candidate expected knowledge breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The average Ph.D. candidate will take about fourteen to eighteen semester courses of undergraduate mathematics and sixteen graduate courses; roughly two shelves of books (about sixty to eighty volumes) should suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a practical benchmark of depth for specialists; across mathematics there are many subspecialties (coarse estimate ~1000; fine structure >3000), so the two-shelf depth sample is a local standard of preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as cumulative but subject to obsolescence
rubrics_metrics.description: While much old and true mathematics is retained in principle, individual facts may be found erroneous, theories may become neglected, applications may become irrelevant, and superior methods replace inferior ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should account for historical change, obsolescence, and reinterpretation; what counts as central knowledge shifts over time (examples: special-function tables replaced by computer approximations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal saturation as a measure of an area's potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Many areas show signs of internal exhaustion—e.g., the elementary geometry of the circle and triangle or the classical theory of functions of a complex variable—and are unlikely to produce startling new results within their bounded confines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of an area’s potential should consider whether the mode of expression admits genuinely new prototypes or is essentially exhausted; this affects where new research is likely to be fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of new mathematical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two inexhaustible sources of new mathematical questions: the development of science and technology, and mathematics itself (each completed result spawns new investigations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating research problems should weigh whether they are driven by external scientific/technological demands or by internal generative properties of mathematics; fruitful problems often arise at intersections of specialties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor and proof as central professional standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal mathematician 'rests his faith on rigorous proof' and regards the difference between a correct proof and an incorrect one as an unmistakable and decisive difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor is the touchstone of mathematical validity, though in practice the boundary of what is 'rigorous' can be fuzzy and controversial; demanding clear proofs remains a core evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional identity measured by field, publication, and peer usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician is labeled by his field, by how much he publishes, and especially by whose work he uses, and by whose taste he follows in his choice of problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These social/professional metrics (field affiliation, publication record, intellectual debts) are commonly used to evaluate standing and influence within the mathematical community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility/intelligibility as a characteristic of work
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal mathematician’s work is intelligible only to a small group of specialists, numbering a few dozen or at most a few hundred; understanding it requires an arduous apprenticeship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing work, consider target audience and accessibility: high-specialization may be acceptable professionally but limits broader comprehension and debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical preservation of the mathematical record
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of mathematical knowledge can occur through destruction of libraries, wars, social upheavals, or deterioration of paper (cheap wood-pulp paper introduced c.1850 self-destructs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of the corpus of mathematics should account for preservation risk; responsible stewardship (archiving, durable media) is part of maintaining the shared standards and history of the field.
